title: Russian Strike on Ukraine Aid Hub Kills 29; US Calls for Fresh Peace Talks
body:
A Russian airstrike on a humanitarian distribution centre in the Zaporizhzhia region killed at least 29 civilians on Saturday, prompting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to denounce the attack as “vile” and to warn that Moscow shows no intention of easing the conflict. The strike comes just hours after Washington announced that it will host a new round of Ukraine‑Russia peace talks on 10‑11 November, a diplomatic effort that many hoped could revive stalled negotiations.

The target was an aid hub operated by the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) and local NGOs, which had been processing and dispatching food, medical supplies and winter clothing to displaced residents of the war‑torn south‑eastern oblast. Ukrainian officials said a Russian missile struck the facility during the early afternoon, igniting a fire that quickly engulfed the makeshift warehouses and killing dozens of people who were waiting for assistance. Rescue crews and volunteers worked through the night to pull survivors from the rubble, while the WFP condemned the strike as a violation of international humanitarian law.

Zelenskyy, speaking from Kyiv, called the bombing “a further proof that Russia does not want any kind of de‑escalation.” He urged the United Nations Security Council to refer the incident to the International Criminal Court, and he appealed to the United States and its allies to increase pressure on Moscow. “When a place meant to save lives becomes a target, the world must see the true nature of this aggression,” he said. The president’s remarks underscore a growing frustration in Kyiv over what it perceives as a pattern of attacks on civilian infrastructure, including power plants, water treatment facilities and now a humanitarian distribution centre.

The United States, meanwhile, announced that Secretary of State Antony Blinken will travel to Geneva for a two‑day summit aimed at restarting peace talks between Kyiv and Moscow. The talks, scheduled for 10‑11 November, will involve senior officials from the United States, European Union and the United Nations, and will seek to build on the “Ukrainian‑Russian dialogue” framework that was first proposed in early 2024. While the Biden administration has emphasized that any negotiations must be predicated on a ceasefire and respect for Ukraine’s sovereignty, critics argue that the timing of the summit—so close to the Zaporizhzhia attack—could undermine its credibility.

Analysts note that the strike may be a calculated move by Moscow to signal that it will not be coerced by diplomatic overtures. “Russia has repeatedly used the threat of escalation to gain leverage at the negotiating table,” said Dr. Elena Morozova, a senior fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations. “Targeting an aid hub not only inflicts civilian casualties but also creates a humanitarian crisis that can be weaponized politically.” The incident also raises questions about the enforcement of the Geneva Conventions, which prohibit attacks on objects indispensable to the survival of the civilian population. International legal experts warn that repeated violations could trigger sanctions or even trigger proceedings at the International Criminal Court, though enforcement mechanisms remain limited.

Humanitarian agencies have warned that the bombing could disrupt the flow of aid to an estimated 1.2 million people in the region who rely on the centre for basic necessities. The WFP announced that it would relocate its operations to a nearby facility, but logistical challenges and security concerns could delay the delivery of critical supplies as winter approaches. The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) called for an immediate “humanitarian pause” to allow safe passage for aid workers and to prevent further loss of life.

Looking ahead, the upcoming peace talks will test the resolve of both sides amid an intensifying humanitarian crisis. If the negotiations succeed, they could pave the way for a ceasefire that would protect civilians and restore vital aid corridors. Conversely, if Moscow continues to target humanitarian sites, the talks risk being derailed, further isolating Russia diplomatically and deepening the suffering of Ukraine’s civilian population. The world now watches closely, hoping that diplomatic engagement can outpace the cycle of violence that has claimed so many lives.
